name: Jabin and Sisera
charge: Mightily oppressing Israel twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron
summary: When Ehud was dead the children of Israel again did evil, and the Lord handed them over to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor, whose captain was Sisera of Harosheth of the Gentiles. Nine hundred chariots of iron, and twenty years of harsh oppression, until Israel cried. The Lord drew Sisera to the river Kishon and routed him and all his army before the sword; heaven itself fought against him and the river swept his army away. He fled on foot and died in a tent, and God subdued Jabin before the children of Israel.
offenseFull: When Ehud was dead the children of Israel again did evil in the Lord’s sight, and He handed them over to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor; his captain was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles (Judges 4:1-3). Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron and harshly oppressed Israel for twenty years, and they cried to the Lord. That is the cycle already laid down in chapter two, running one more turn: Israel does evil, is sold into an oppressor’s hand, cries out, and a deliverer is raised up.

The song of that day describes what the servitude did to ordinary life. The highways were empty and travellers kept to back paths, and village life ceased in Israel until Deborah arose, a mother in Israel; and it names the cause underneath it, that the people took up new gods and war arrived at their gates, with forty thousand in Israel and no shield or spear among them (Judges 5:6-8). The iron chariots account for the terror of it; they do not account for how Israel came to be under them. Sisera is the general of the Canaanite host, and Israel had been told plainly not to fear horses and chariots and an army larger than their own, because the Lord their God was with them (Deuteronomy 20:1). The fear came in because the faith had gone out.
judgmentFull: Deborah gave Barak the Lord’s command: march to mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and the Lord would draw Sisera with his chariots and his army to the river Kishon and give him into Barak’s hand (Judges 4:6-7). Sisera gathered all nine hundred chariots of iron and all his people to the river, and Deborah told Barak the day had come and the Lord had gone out ahead of him. The Lord threw Sisera, his chariots and his whole army into a rout before Barak’s sword, so that Sisera jumped down from his chariot and fled on foot, and the whole army fell by the sword until not one man was left (Judges 4:12-16).

The song tells how it was done. The kings of Canaan fought by the waters of Megiddo and carried off no silver as plunder; heaven itself fought, the stars from their courses battled Sisera, and the ancient river Kishon swept them away (Judges 5:19-21). Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, because Jabin king of Hazor was at peace with Heber’s house, and he died there with a tent peg through his temple; so God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan that day before Israel, and Israel pressed harder and harder against him until they had destroyed him (Judges 4:17-24). The song closes at a window in Harosheth: Sisera’s mother looked out and cried, asking why his chariot was so slow in coming, and her wisest ladies answered her with imagined victory, that they were dividing the spoils. She was looking for a son who was never coming home; he lay dead in Jael’s tent. The song ends by wishing ruin on the Lord’s enemies and the strength of the rising sun on those who love Him; and the land had rest forty years (Judges 5:28-31).

text.text: And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, when Ehud was dead.
And the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles.
And the children of Israel cried unto the Lord: for he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel.
In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways.
The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods; then was war in the gates: was there a shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?

When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.

And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedesh–naphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?
And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand.
And they shewed Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam was gone up to mount Tabor.
And Sisera gathered together all his chariots, even nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people that were with him, from Harosheth of the Gentiles unto the river of Kishon.

And Deborah said unto Barak, Up; for this is the day in which the Lord hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the Lord gone out before thee? So Barak went down from mount Tabor, and ten thousand men after him.
And the Lord discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots, and all his host, with the edge of the sword before Barak; so that Sisera lighted down off his chariot, and fled away on his feet.
But Barak pursued after the chariots, and after the host, unto Harosheth of the Gentiles: and all the host of Sisera fell upon the edge of the sword; and there was not a man left.
The kings came and fought, then fought the kings of Canaan in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo; they took no gain of money.
They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.
The river of Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength.
Howbeit Sisera fled away on his feet to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite: for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.
And Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said unto him, Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not. And when he had turned in unto her into the tent, she covered him with a mantle.
And he said unto her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink; for I am thirsty. And she opened a bottle of milk, and gave him drink, and covered him.
Again he said unto her, Stand in the door of the tent, and it shall be, when any man doth come and enquire of thee, and say, Is there any man here? that thou shalt say, No.

Then Jael Heber’s wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died.

And, behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him, and said unto him, Come, and I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest. And when he came into her tent, behold, Sisera lay dead, and the nail was in his temples.
So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel.
And the hand of the children of Israel prospered, and prevailed against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?
Her wise ladies answered her, yea, she returned answer to herself,

Have they not sped? have they not divided the prey; to every man a damsel or two; to Sisera a prey of divers colours, a prey of divers colours of needlework, of divers colours of needlework on both sides, meet for the necks of them that take the spoil?
So let all thine enemies perish, O Lord: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.
